top.headline: Gavin Newsom Commutes California's Entire Death Row, the Largest in the Western Hemisphere
top.blurb: Newsom commuted the sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life without parole, writing that 'state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values.' The state has not executed anyone since 2006; his successor, Xavier Becerra, has pledged to extend the moratorium, while the US has executed 33 people elsewhere so far this year.

top.headline: The DOJ Civil Rights Official Who Spent 19 Months Targeting Colleges Is Resigning
top.blurb: Harmeet Dhillon is stepping down as the Justice Department's assistant attorney general for civil rights after opening more than 100 investigations into university admissions and pursuing two dismissed lawsuits against Harvard. Critics say the division stopped investigating systemic racism and sexism claims under her tenure; more than 300 colleges have dropped or altered DEI policies since 2024.

top.headline: Democrats Vow to Investigate Corruption — Except the Colleague Trump Pardoned
top.blurb: As Democrats pledge to probe Trump-era corruption, none of their announced inquiries name Rep. Henry Cuellar, who Trump pardoned last year after prosecutors charged him with taking $600,000 in bribes tied to his Appropriations Committee seat. Cuellar won re-election with 66% of the vote Tuesday and is positioned to chair a subcommittee overseeing Homeland Security funding.

top.headline: Fake Takedown Notices Impersonating the RSS and Delhi Police Targeted Digital Rights Groups
top.blurb: Scroll traced legal notices demanding the Internet Freedom Foundation and SFLC delete posts — one purporting to be from the RSS, another a fake Delhi Police report to X — to a Proton Mail address created hours before, with no court order backing the claimed defamation charge. X told the Delhi High Court on Friday that an imposter, not the police, had filed the takedown request.

top.headline: Six Non-Muslim Communities Must Now Get Visas to Stay in India, Reversing a Blanket Exemption
top.blurb: The home ministry amended its 2025 exemption order so Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Christians, Jains and Parsis who entered India without valid papers from Afghanistan, Bangladesh or Pakistan before 2025 must now obtain a visa to keep living here, aligning the rule with the 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act's religion-based fast track to citizenship.

top.headline: Karnataka High Court Quashes BJP's Defamation Case Over Congress's '40% Commission' Ads
top.blurb: The court threw out a criminal defamation complaint the BJP filed against Rahul Gandhi, Siddaramaiah and DK Shivakumar over 2023 campaign ads branding the Bommai government a '40% commission sarkar' and alleging a Rs 1,500 crore corruption racket. The BJP had called the allegations the product of 'fanciful imagination'; the court had already stayed proceedings against each petitioner over the past year.

top.headline: Trump Says a Russia-Ukraine Deal Is Near After Melania Trump Hosts Both Sides at the White House
top.blurb: Trump predicted a 'big agreement' involving 'more than Ukraine' after meeting Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev, hours after the First Lady hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials together — a first, the White House says — building on a six-day truce she helped broker that let nearly 800 civilians evacuate Oleshky.

top.headline: Iran's Security Chief Delivers Khamenei Letter to Putin as Tehran Holds the Line on US Talks
top.blurb: Mohsen Rezaei told Putin that Moscow backs ending US 'aggression' against Iran and discussed a proposed Russia-Iran gas pipeline, as Khamenei rejected any 'inclination towards submission' to Washington. Rezaei said Tehran won't negotiate on the war or reopening the Strait of Hormuz until the US meets its seven conditions, even as Trump's party lost both chambers of Congress partly over war-driven prices.

top.headline: Armed Israeli Settlers Seize Eight Palestinian Homes Near Jericho, Displacing Dozens
top.blurb: About 30 settlers tied to the annexationist group Nachala took over homes in Ein a-Duyuk a-Tahta, with the UN saying they used live ammunition and assaulted residents; Palestinian officials call the settlers' purchase documents forged. The Israeli military has since sealed the area as a closed military zone, blocking humanitarian access to displaced families.

top.headline: Debutant Wickham and Centurion Jangoo Rebuild West Indies After Early Collapse in Sylhet
top.blurb: West Indies slumped to three quick wickets against Bangladesh's pace attack before Kevin Wickham, debuting after injuries ruled out two openers, and Amir Jangoo added 131 for the fourth wicket. Jangoo reached his second Test century and finished day one unbeaten on 111, with Justin Greaves also unbeaten as West Indies closed on 235/4.

more.headline: Afghanistan Leaves the Door Open for Rashid Khan's Test Return
more.blurb: Afghanistan's setup says it would welcome Rashid Khan back in Test cricket despite his focus on white-ball formats in recent years, as the board weighs squad depth ahead of its next red-ball assignments.

top.headline: 'Dilwali Diwali' Review: A Promising Idea About Gentrification, Over Almost Before It Starts
top.blurb: Nandini Ramnath reviews Ritesh Menon's Netflix short about parents who sneak back to their old Mumbai flat rather than live in the upscale apartment their engineer son abroad bought them. She praises Manoj Pahwa and Neelu Kohli's performances but says the 61-minute film reads like an early draft, leaving its ideas about class and gentrification unexplored.

bengal.headline: Calcutta High Court Asked to Probe Whether Bengal's MBBS 'Donor Quota' Bypassed Merit
bengal.blurb: A rejected medical aspirant alleges the state Health department and WBMCC filled seats offline through a secretive 'donor quota' tied to private trusts, bypassing higher-ranked NEET candidates in violation of National Medical Commission rules.

bengal.headline: Calcutta HC Blocks Deportation of Indian Passport-Holding Mother and Children to Bangladesh
bengal.blurb: A vacation bench ruled that a woman and her two children, detained near the border as suspected Bangladeshi nationals, cannot be pushed back before their Indian passports are lawfully cancelled, ordering them produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

travel.headline: Georgia's Okefenokee Swamp Becomes the First US Wildlife Refuge Named a UNESCO World Heritage Site
travel.blurb: UNESCO inscribed the 400,000-acre Okefenokee refuge, home to over 1,270 species and likely the world's largest intact subtropical peatland, after a four-decade nomination effort that also helped block a proposed titanium mine on its hydrological boundary.

travel.headline: Horseshoe Crabs Confirmed in a Second Philippine Province After Interviews With 142 Residents
travel.blurb: Researchers confirmed two horseshoe crab species, including an IUCN-endangered one, living in Tawi-Tawi's waters for the first time, after residents reported them for medicinal and ritual uses and said numbers are falling to harvesting and pollution.

happy.headline: At a Montana Guest Ranch, Autistic Adults Aren't Guests — They're the Wranglers, Guides and Cooks
happy.blurb: Kathryn Nordberg opened Erik's Ranch near Yellowstone in 2014, naming it for her autistic son, to give neurodivergent adults paid work and a home as they aged out of school support. Staff live in cabins designed against sensory overload, one member runs a baking business from a picture-labeled recipe book, and another keeps hens she named after puns — a small operation Nordberg says will 'never be huge,' but has now employed 27 people.

tech_top.headline: Independent Auditor Finds Anthropic's AI Research Has Roughly Doubled in Speed Since Late 2025
tech_top.pm_note: This is a third party, not a vendor blog post, measuring 'AI accelerating AI R&D' directly — and even it says the public has to take Anthropic's redactions on faith. Expect 'independently audited acceleration' to become a real diligence question for any AI-heavy roadmap.
tech_top.blurb: METR's 11-week assessment estimates Anthropic's internal model capabilities are improving at about 1.9x the 2024-2025 rate, with roughly 80% of that acceleration attributable to AI use rather than more compute. Anthropic held unilateral redaction rights and cut most of the evidence METR found most informative, which METR says forces outsiders to 'rely on our judgment much more than would be ideal.'

tech_top.headline: Meta Pauses a Plan to Train AI on Business Customers' Website Content After Backlash
tech_top.pm_note: A Norwegian court injunction and a UK antitrust probe killed this before it even launched — when a ToS change reaches into customers' own domains for training data, expect regulators to move faster than your rollout timeline.
tech_top.blurb: Meta indefinitely paused a November 20 update to its commercial terms that would have let it use business accounts' website content to train its AI products, after the Los Angeles Times broke the story, a Norwegian court granted an injunction backed by 180 media companies, and the UK's competition authority opened its own inquiry. Meta says it is still 'consulting stakeholders' before deciding what comes next.

tech_more.headline: He Built an AI Tool That Mass-Produced Fake IDs. Now He's Telling His Story.
tech_more.blurb: Yuriy Nazarenko's OnlyFake service used generative AI to auto-produce realistic fake IDs for $15 each, earning over $1 million before the FBI caught him; North Korean fake-IT-worker operations used his tools, and he served about a year in US prison before landing in ICE detention.

tech_101.text: How much faster an AI system's measured abilities are improving compared to its historical pace — expressed as a multiple, like '2x,' meaning a year of normal progress now happens in six months. It's the metric at the center of worries about AI improving itself faster than anyone can oversee.

The identity verification banks and financial platforms are legally required to run before opening an account, meant to block fraud and money laundering. AI-generated fake IDs are a growing threat to KYC because they can be mass-produced cheaply enough to overwhelm manual review.

science.headline: A Room-Temperature Membrane Could Replace the Heat-Hungry Step at the Heart of Oil Refining
science.blurb: KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers built a cheap polymer membrane whose pores clog with heavy hydrocarbons in exactly the way needed to separate crude oil without the 350°C heat distillation requires. Simulations suggest refinery-wide adoption could cut energy use by 32% and emissions by 38%; the membrane held up over 28 days on real crude but hasn't been tested at refinery scale.

science.headline: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Takes Its First Clear Look at the Asteroid NASA Deliberately Struck
science.blurb: Hera photographed Didymos and its small moon Dimorphos as separate objects for the first time from 1,280 km away, four years after NASA's DART probe slammed into Dimorphos and shortened its orbit by 33 minutes — far more than simulations predicted. The spacecraft will soon release two CubeSats to examine the impact site up close and settle whether DART left a crater.

science.headline: A Narrow Loophole Might Let a Fast-Spinning Black Hole Split in Two
science.blurb: Physicists modeling black hole thermodynamics found that splitting normally destroys entropy and is forbidden — but extremely fast rotation could open a narrow exception, provided the resulting fragments move apart instead of re-merging. No split has been observed, and the team says they can't yet assign the scenario a probability, but gamma-ray telescopes could one day catch indirect signs of it.

philosophy.headline: A Philosopher's Father, a Lifetime of Reading Socrates, and the Death Neither Prepared Him For
philosophy.blurb: Scott F. Parker reflects on his father, a philosophy professor whose childhood OCD was eased by the discipline he later taught, and whether a life spent with Socrates, Montaigne and memento mori could prepare him to let go of his own failing body. He finds that philosophy's comfort may serve the survivors more than the dying, since cognitive decline left his father unable to draw on what he'd spent decades preparing.

philosophy.headline: When Every Side Has Its Story: Why Relativism Is the Wrong Answer to Propaganda
philosophy.blurb: Mohsen Askari, an Iranian exile in Istanbul, argues that incompatible accounts of events back home don't mean all narratives are equally true — some conceal harm and some expose it. Drawing on Arendt and Fricker's idea of testimonial injustice, he proposes judging rival narratives by what facts they must deny and whose suffering they erase, rather than shrugging that 'every side has its truth.'

philosophy_101.text: Latin for 'remember you will die' — a practice, going back to the Stoics, of deliberately keeping mortality in mind as a way to clarify what matters now, rather than as a source of despair.

Philosopher Miranda Fricker's term for when someone's word is given less credibility than it deserves because of prejudice against who they are — a mechanism authoritarian regimes exploit by recasting credible witnesses as 'infiltrators' or 'saboteurs.'
